Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 89, verse 1–5:

Meccan, and its verses are 30 (some say 29) [revealed after the night]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by the dawn, just as He swears by the morning in His saying: ﴿And by the morning when it brightens﴾ and ﴿By the morning when it breathes﴾. It is also said: by the prayer of dawn. By "the ten nights" He means the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. If you ask: why is it indefinite (nakira) among the things He swears by? I say: because they are specific nights distinguished from the category of nights in general, the ten being a part of them; or because they are specified with a virtue not possessed by others. If you ask: why was it not defined with the definite article of prior reference (lam al-ahd), since they are known and well-established nights? I say: had that been done, it would not have been self-sufficient in conveying the sense of excellence that lies in the indefiniteness; and because it is better for the definite articles to be uniform, so that the speech is further from riddles and obscurity. And by "the even and the odd": either all things, their even and their odd, or the even and odd of these nights. It is permissible that its even is the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr) and its odd is the Day of Arafah, since it is the ninth of its days and that is its tenth. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he explained them as such [[I say: the reasoning is from the words of al-Zamakhshari. Its origin is in al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, al-Bazzar, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, the twenty-third (section), from the narration of Khayr ibn Nu'aym from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir. He said: we do not know it except with this chain.]].

They have multiplied (the views) on the even and the odd until they nearly exhausted the categories of what they may refer to, and that is of little benefit, worthy of being neglected. After swearing by the specific nights, He swears by the night in general: ﴿when it passes﴾, i.e. when it goes by, like His saying ﴿And the night when it turns its back﴾ and ﴿And the night when it darkens﴾. It was also read: "wal-witr" with a fatha on the waw; both are dialects, like "al-hibr" and "al-hibr" in the sense of number (ʿadad); and for "al-tirah" (vengeance) only the kasra is used. Also read: "al-witr" with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ta', related by Yunus from Abu 'Amr. Also read: "wal-fajr, wal-witr, wa-yasr" with tanwin, which is the tanwin that falls as a substitute for the vowel-lengthening letter. From Ibn 'Abbas: "wa-layali 'ashr" with the idafa, meaning "wa-layali ayyam 'ashr" (and nights of ten days). The ya' of ﴿yasri﴾ is dropped in continuous speech, being replaced by the kasra; and when pausing, it is dropped together with the kasra. It was also said: the meaning of "yasra" is "yusra fihi" (it proceeds in it). ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding (hijr)?﴾ i.e., in what He has sworn by of these things, is there an oath (qasam), meaning a thing sworn by, for one of understanding? He means: is it fitting in his sight that it be magnified by swearing by them? Or: is my swearing by them for one of understanding, i.e. is it a great oath with which the sworn matter is emphasized? "Al-hijr" means intellect, because it restrains (yahjur) one from rushing into what is not fitting, just as it is called "aql" (restraint/binding) and "nuha" (restraint), because it binds and restrains. "Hijr" is from "ihsa'" (counting/regulating), which means control. Al-Farra' said: it is said, "He is possessed of hijr" when he is dominant over himself, controlling it. The sworn-to matter is omitted, and it is "la-yu'adhdhabanna" (surely they will be punished), indicated by His saying ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad?﴾ down to His saying ﴿so your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 89, verse 6–14:

It was said that the descendants of ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh were called ʿĀd, just as the descendants of Banu Hashim are called Hashim. Then the earliest of them were called ʿĀd al-Ūlā (the First ʿĀd) and Iram, naming them after their forefather, and those after them were called ʿĀd al-Akhīra (the Last ʿĀd). Ibn al-Ruqayyat said:

"A glory ancient, whose first ancestors built it, who reached ʿĀd and, before him, Iram."

[[Ibn al-Ruqayyat, describing a man who had attained an ancient glory. That is: of old. He likened it to a fortress built on the path of metonymy (al-makniyya), and "built" is an imaginative expression (takhyīl), meaning: its founders and first ancestors initiated and renewed it. The forefathers of the one being praised reached this glory through ʿĀd and, before him, Iram. Before ʿĀd means before ʿĀd (the son of ʿAwṣ), since he is ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. So the descendants of this ʿĀd are the First ʿĀd, and those after them are the Second ʿĀd.]]

In His saying "with ʿĀd, Iram" (bi-ʿĀdin Iram), Iram is in apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to ʿĀd, and it indicates that they are the First ʿĀd, the ancient ones. It was also said that Iram is the name of their town and land in which they lived, and the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr supports this: "bi-ʿĀd Iram," with an idāfa (genitive construction). Its meaning is: "with ʿĀd, the people of Iram," as in His saying "and ask the town" (wa-s'alil-qaryata). It is not declined, whether it is a tribe or a land, because of definiteness and feminine gender.

Al-Ḥasan read "bi-ʿĀd Iram" with both letters fatḥa. It was also read "bi-ʿĀd Irm" with the rāʾ sukūn for lightening, as it was read "bi-warqikum" (with your silver). It was read "bi-ʿĀd Iram dhāt al-ʿimād," with Iram in construct with dhāt al-ʿimād. Al-Iram means a landmark, so the meaning is: "with ʿĀd, the people of the landmarks of dhāt al-ʿimād." Dhāt al-ʿImād is the name of the city. It was also read "bi-ʿĀd Irram dhāt al-ʿimād," meaning that God made dhāt al-ʿimād into rubble (rimām) in place of the act of your Lord. If dhāt al-ʿimād is an attribute of the tribe, the meaning is that they were nomads, people of pillars, or tall of body, likening their frames to pillars. From this comes the saying "a man muʿammad" and "ʿumdān," meaning tall. It was also said: "possessor of the elevated building." If it is an attribute of the town, the meaning is that it had pillars.

It is reported that ʿĀd had two sons, Shaddād and Shadīd, who ruled and dominated. Then Shadīd died and the affair passed entirely to Shaddād, who ruled the world, and its kings submitted to him. He heard the mention of Paradise and said: "Shall I build one like it?" So he built Iram in some deserts of Aden over three hundred years, while his lifespan was nine hundred years. It was a great city whose palaces were of gold and silver, and whose pillars were of chrysolite and ruby. In it were kinds of trees and flowing rivers. When its construction was complete, he set out toward it with the people of his kingdom. When he was one day and night's journey away from it, God sent upon them a cry from the sky, and they perished. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilaba that he went out seeking camels of his, came upon it, and carried away what he could of what was there. His report reached Muʿāwiya, who summoned him, and he related the story to him. Muʿāwiya sent for Kaʿb and asked him, and he said: "It is Iram dhāt al-ʿimād." [[Al-Tha'labi reported it through ʿUthman al-Darimi, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Salih, from Abu Lahiʿa, from Khalid ibn Abi ʿImran, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilaba, that he went out seeking camels of his that had strayed, and mentioned it at length. I say: signs of fabrication are evident in it.]] "And a man from the Muslims will enter it in your time, reddish-blond, short, with a mole on his eyebrow and a mole on his heel, who will go out seeking camels of his." Then he turned and saw Ibn Qilaba and said: "This is that man, by God." "Which had not been created like it in the lands" (lam yukhlaq mithluhā): like ʿĀd in the lands, great in bodily size and strength. A man among them was four hundred cubits tall, and he would come to a huge rock, carry it, and throw it onto the tribe, destroying them. Or: "such as had not been created like the city of Shaddād in all the lands of the world." Ibn al-Zubayr read "lam yukhlaq mithlahā," meaning: God did not create its like.

"Who hewed the rock" (jābū al-ṣakhr): they cut the rocks of the mountains and made houses in them, as in His saying "and you hew out of the mountains houses" (wa-tanḥitūna min al-jibāli buyūtan). It was said: the first to hew mountains, rocks, and marble were Thamūd, and they built one thousand seven hundred cities, all of stone.

He was called "Dhū al-Awtād" (possessor of the stakes) because of the abundance of his troops and the tent-pegs they drove when they camped, or because he tortured with stakes, as he did to the hairdresser of his daughter and to Āsiya.

"Who transgressed" (alladhīna ṭaghaw): the best view regarding it is that it is in the accusative position as a disparagement. It may also be nominative: "they are those who transgressed," or genitive, as a description of those mentioned: ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh.

It is said: "he poured the whip upon him, covered him and enveloped him." Mentioning the whip indicates that what He inflicted upon them in this world of great punishment, compared to what He prepared for them in the Hereafter, is like a whip compared to all other things by which one is punished. It is reported from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd that when al-Ḥasan came upon this verse he would say: "Indeed with God there are many whips, and He seized them with one of them."

"Al-Mirṣād" (the place of watching): the place where surveillance is established, a form of "mifʿāl" from "raṣada" (to watch), like "al-mīqāt" from "waqqata" (to set a time). This is a metaphor for His watching over the disobedient with punishment, and that they cannot escape Him. It is reported from some Arabs that someone asked him: "Where is your Lord?" He said: "At the watchpost."

It is reported from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him, that he recited this surah in the presence of some tyrants until he reached this verse, and said: "Indeed your Lord is at the watchpost, O so-and-so," alluding in this address to the fact that he was one of the tyrants who had threatened with that. It is the believing soul, or the soul at rest in the truth, in which the coolness of certainty has settled so that no doubt stirs in it. The first explanation is supported by the recitation (*qira'a*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "O soul that is secure and at rest."

If you ask, "When is she told this?" I answer: either at death, or at the resurrection, or at entry into Paradise. The meaning is:

﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ (by "your Lord's appointment," in the sense of the commentary's reading), ﴿and enter among My servants﴾, among the righteous servants, and join their ranks, ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾ with them.

It is also said that the *nafs* here is the spirit (*rūḥ*). Its meaning is: "Enter into the bodies of My servants." Ibn Abbas recited: "fa-dkhulī fī ʿabdī" (فادخلي في عبدى). Ibn Mas'ud recited: "fī jasad ʿabdī" (في جسد عبدى). Ubayy recited: "ītī rabbiki rāḍiya marḍiyya. Udkhulī fī ʿabdī" (ائتى ربك راضية مرضية. ادخلى في عبدى).

It is also said that it was revealed concerning Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.
